TOPIC_REFERENCE: B-Tree Indexes — Storage Layout and Kernel Boundary
SECTION_TITLE: Where Storage Sits: Page Boundaries, Buffer Pools, and Node Fanout
SECTION_BODY:
To understand how an indexing structure survives at scale, we must look at where data lives across the hardware and operating system boundary. An index is not an abstract algorithmic tree floating in memory; it is a physical on-disk data structure pinned to block boundaries.

Operating system kernels and storage hardware do not read and write individual bytes; they transfer data in fixed-size blocks (typically 4 Kilobytes (4 KB) or 8 KB). A database engine manages these blocks via an internal memory cache called the Buffer Pool💡 Buffer PoolDatabase SubsystemA dedicated region of physical memory allocated by the database server to cache disk pages in RAM. When a query needs data, the engine first checks if the page is resident in the buffer pool before issuing an expensive storage read..

💡 Intuitive Mental Model: The Nested Card Catalog Memory Hierarchy

Imagine a vast library with 10 million books. If the librarian had to inspect every shelf sequentially from entrance to back exit, locating one title would take days.

A B-tree index acts like a hierarchical card catalog. The top card lists 100 room doors; each room has a card listing 100 cabinets; each cabinet holds 100 shelves. By reading only 3 cards (the root, intermediate branch, and leaf), the librarian pinpoints the exact shelf in seconds—even though the building holds millions of books.

In a B-tree, this hierarchy is governed by node Fanout💡 Node FanoutTree GeometryThe number of child pointers held inside a single branch node. In an 8 KB database page, a fanout of 100 to 500 child pointers means a tree with only 3 to 4 levels can index hundreds of millions of rows.. When nodes are traversed in RAM, the database engine uses Pointer Swizzling💡 Pointer SwizzlingEngine OptimizationThe performance technique of replacing on-disk page identifiers (like File 3, Page 1290) with direct 64-bit RAM memory pointers once a page is loaded into the buffer pool, bypassing subsequent hash table lookups during tree traversal. to transform disk offsets into raw memory pointers.
